id: [Were it but Me that gained the Height—]

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

World like a coat, silver clasps, ermine lined, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in the red center—I thought everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket amongst the butterscotch candies, the matchbooks? Unessential but accounted for, a steady thing to touch. World like a morning glory, withered every evening, world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. When anyone questioned me, I held it forth, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. World like an egret, still and white on the highway divider, world like a regret typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing, I cannot hold you at all, it seems, your evergreens, your curling potato vine; it’s all too much much, and I a bit of goosedown, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra, the world like a world like a world.

prompts.L3:

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker reflects on lost faith, sobriety, and belonging through a cascade of shifting similes that portray the world as comforting, fearful, beautiful, and fragile. The collapse of belief leaves the speaker exposed and unaccounted for, revealing how meaning once provided a protective shape against an overwhelming world.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: World, Unessential, When

outputs.L1: World like a coat, silver-clasped and ermine-lined, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in the red center—I thought everything had a purpose. This was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket among the butterscotch candies and matchbooks? Unessential but accounted for, a steady thing to touch. World like a morning glory, withered every evening; world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how deeply I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. Whenever anyone questioned me, I held it forth and let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. World like an egret, still and white on the highway divider; world like a regret, typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing. I cannot hold you at all, it seems: your evergreens, your curling potato vine. It’s all too much, much—and I, a bit of goose down, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra—the world like a world like a world.
outputs.L2:
The earth seemed like an overcoat fastened with pewter buckles, fur-trimmed and heated by the bodies buried within, circling a crimson core. In those days, when alcohol was still part of my life, I believed every object and event had its reason. I imagined myself a privileged passenger tucked into a pocket beside caramel sweets and little books of matches: unnecessary, perhaps, yet included in the count, something reliable beneath the fingers.

The world opened like a flower at dawn and collapsed by nightfall; it cowered like a dog with raised fur at the sound of a storm. Now I’m astonished by the force of my former faith—how it fitted itself to me, molded itself to my warmth, and hardened into something almost physical. If someone doubted me, I presented that conviction like a garment and invited them to feel its fabric. I considered myself complete.

The world appeared as a motionless white heron standing in the median of a road, or as remorse written on a page and deleted. I cannot draw you nearer without making our closeness visible to everyone; apparently, I cannot embrace you whatsoever. Your conifers and twisting potato creeper overwhelm me. Beside them, I am only a loose feather or drifting thistledown—bareheaded, exposed, omitted from the tally, wholly superfluous—while the world keeps resembling itself, again and again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker once believed that everything in the world had a purpose and that they occupied a secure, if modest, place within a larger order. This conviction surrounded and protected them, becoming so powerful that it felt almost tangible—a shelter built from certainty and meaning.

After quitting drinking, however, the speaker looks back with astonishment at how completely they once trusted this vision. The world now appears unstable and elusive, revealed through shifting images of beauty and fear, decay and stillness, longing and regret. What once seemed coherent no longer offers comfort or explanation.

As a result, the speaker feels unable to draw the world close or claim a meaningful place within it. Instead, they experience themselves as exposed and weightless, suspended without protection, purpose, or recognition—as though they have slipped beyond the boundaries of what can be counted or accounted for.
outputs.L4:
The speaker looks back on the loss of faith not as a single moment of rejection, but as a gradual change in how the world feels and how the self fits within it. Sobriety intensifies this experience by removing another form of shelter. Without belief or intoxication to soften reality, the speaker must confront life directly, searching for a place of belonging in a world that seems to change each time it is described.

A cascade of shifting similes captures this instability. The world appears by turns comforting and threatening, beautiful and terrifying, solid and easily broken. Each comparison briefly offers a way to understand experience, yet no image remains sufficient for long. The repeated movement from one likeness to another suggests that language itself is struggling to contain what the speaker feels. Reality cannot be reduced to a single meaning: it invites wonder while also producing fear, and it can seem welcoming at one moment and indifferent the next.

The collapse of belief therefore leaves the speaker exposed. Faith once provided an organizing structure—a protective shape that gave suffering, identity, and belonging a place within a larger design. When that structure disappears, the speaker no longer feels recognized or accounted for by the universe. Sobriety reinforces this vulnerability, because there is no easy means of escape from the uncertainty. The speaker must remain fully present before a world whose vastness can be both exhilarating and unbearable.

Yet the reflection is not simply a lament for lost belief. The speaker’s shifting images also reveal a continued desire to make meaning, even after certainty has vanished. The act of comparing, describing, and reconsidering the world becomes a new way of engaging with it. Although the speaker can no longer rely on faith as a secure enclosure, the search for language and connection persists. Meaning may no longer feel permanent or divinely guaranteed, but it can still be created through attention, honesty, and the difficult effort to belong within a fragile and overwhelming reality.
outputs.L5:
### When the World Becomes Unessential

There are moments when the world feels immense—full of urgent voices, crowded streets, unfinished plans, and expectations. Then something happens: a quiet sunrise, a familiar hand in yours, a breath taken after fear. Suddenly, much of what seemed important becomes unessential.

When noise fades, we remember that life is not measured only by achievement or attention. It is also found in pauses, in kindness, and in the simple certainty of being present.

The world will continue to hurry. But sometimes, when we stop, we discover what truly matters.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about losing faith in the world after giving up drinking, using surreal similes, intimate imagery, and long, breathless sentences.
counterfactuals.output:
When I stopped drinking, the world did not brighten, it only took off its borrowed jewelry and stood before me shivering, thin as a saint’s wrist, while morning came through the blinds in pale surgical strips and laid its cold hands across the bed where I slept alone, my mouth tasting of pennies and old prayers, my heart knocking softly in its cupboard like something ashamed to be alive.

I had believed sobriety would be a country of clean rivers, but the rivers were mirrors dragged through mud, and every face leaning over them wore my eyes, those two exhausted animals that had followed me home through years of neon rain, through kitchens where I poured oblivion into a glass and watched it bloom like a black flower, through nights when your shoulder beside me was the last warm continent and I kissed the small freckle there as if it were a door.

Now the hours arrive without veils, immense and colorless, each one a horse made of hospital sheets, each one breathing against the window, and I have nowhere to hide from the terrible ordinariness of spoons, bills, birds repeating their bright mechanical lies in the gutters, neighbors carrying groceries beneath a sky that hangs above us like a blue bruise no one admits to seeing.

I wash my hands and remember all they have held—your hair, a sweating tumbler, the sink at three in the morning, my own face lowered into them like a drowned moon—and the water runs clear, which feels like mockery, because clarity is not mercy, clarity is the knife that says here is the wound, here is its true depth, here is the world continuing without kneeling.

Still, at night, I press my palm to my chest and feel the stubborn engine there, small and furious as a moth trapped in a church, and I do not call it hope, not yet, but I listen to it beating beneath the silence, while beyond the glass the city flickers like a dying constellation, every window briefly golden, every stranger carrying their private ruin from room to room, and for one breathless moment I almost believe that faith was never the light at all, but the hand trembling in darkness, refusing to let go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph poem that begins with “World like a coat” and repeatedly uses the phrase “world like,” exploring belief, sobriety, grief, and the feeling of no longer belonging.
counterfactuals.output: World like a coat I once wore without thinking, world like a chapel where belief kept flickering after the candles drowned, world like a glass set down untouched, sobriety bright and bitter on my tongue, world like a letter grief keeps opening with my hands, world like a house whose rooms remember me but will not let me sleep, world like a name I answer to from habit, world like a country seen through the rain of a departing train, and I, unbuttoned from every promise, stand in the cold doorway, listening for a welcome that no longer knows my voice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose poem in a confessional voice. Include silver clasps, butterscotch candies, matchbooks, an egret on a highway divider, evergreens, and thistle fluff.
counterfactuals.output:
I confess: I kept the silver clasps after the dress was gone. They clicked in my palm like tiny teeth, like a language for fastening what had already fled.

In the glove compartment: butterscotch candies furred with age, matchbooks from restaurants I loved only because you were across the table. I struck one once, just to watch a little room disappear.

On the highway divider, an egret stood white and impossible among the exhaust—one clean thought I could not bear to have. Traffic divided around it. I did not.

Beyond the guardrail, evergreens rehearsed their dark permanence. I wanted to join them, to become sharp-scented, snow-proof, unnamed. Instead I opened the window and let thistle fluff enter the car, each seed carrying its soft catastrophe.

This is what I have not told anyone: I mistook leaving for motion. I mistook sweetness for mercy. I still keep fire in small cardboard houses.

Some nights I fasten the air with those silver clasps.

Some nights it holds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic, image-rich monologue in which the speaker remembers once believing everything had a purpose but now feels fragile and unaccounted for. Use clothing and natural imagery throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to believe the world was stitched with intention—that every sorrow was a dark button fastening some larger coat, every joy a bright thread drawn through the hem. Even the rain seemed measured then, each drop assigned to a leaf, a roof, a waiting mouth of earth. I wore my days like a well-made dress: certain the seams would hold, certain someone had chosen the pattern.

Now the lining has come loose.

I wake feeling like a glove left on a winter fence, shaped for a hand that has forgotten it. The wind turns me inside out. Thistles catch at my sleeves; fog gathers at my collar. No one comes to claim me from the field.

Once, I could look at the bare trees and call them patient. I could see purpose in their black branches, how they lifted their emptiness toward spring. But lately they resemble ruined umbrellas, abandoned beneath a colorless sky. Their bark peels like old cuffs. Their roots clutch the cold ground without explanation.

I am fragile in the way moth wings are fragile—not because they lack beauty, but because beauty has not spared them. A touch leaves dust behind. A light can be mistaken for salvation.

Perhaps that is what frightens me most: not that I have suffered, but that the suffering may belong to no design. That no hidden tailor bends over the night, mending what has torn. That I am only this small, fraying thing beneath the weather, with pockets full of dead leaves and no name written inside my coat.

Still, when evening settles its blue shawl across the hills, I sometimes stand very quietly. Snow begins to fall, soft as lint, covering every path that failed to lead me home. For a moment, the whole world looks forgiven.

But I know how easily it will melt.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a surreal literary passage about trying—and failing—to hold the world close. Make the syntax associative and flowing, with recurring metaphors, self-corrections, and an ending that dissolves into repetition.
counterfactuals.output:
I tried to hold the world close, though close is not the word; close is a door persuaded shut, and the world had no door, only weather, only a blue animal turning in its sleep. I put my arms around the morning. My hands met behind its back and came away full of birds.

No, not birds—receipts, perhaps, for purchases I could not remember: one river, three eclipses, a small country of salt. The ink ran down my wrists. Everywhere, the world was itemizing itself, charging me for the light on the kitchen floor, for the pear ripening toward its bruise, for the dust that rose when I said my own name too loudly.

I thought: if I make myself larger, the world will fit inside me.

So I swallowed a road. It curled beneath my tongue and went on for years. I swallowed a church bell, but it rang in my ribs until every silence limped. I swallowed the sea—no, I only drank from a glass left sweating beside the bed, but that night whales moved through my veins, slow as forgotten thoughts, and the moon washed up behind my eyes.

Still the world escaped. It leaked from the seams of things. It poured out of shoes, keyholes, sleeping mouths. Each time I cupped my hands around it, it became smaller and farther away: a coin at the bottom of a well, a pupil narrowing against love, a blue animal turning, always turning, in a room without walls.

Wait, I said. I have not held you yet.

The mountains shrugged off my fingers. The cities shook themselves like wet dogs. Even the dead refused my embrace, slipping through me with the cool politeness of smoke. I tried to gather them back by naming them, but every name opened into another name, and that name into a corridor, and the corridor into weather.

Then I understood—or mistook understanding for another form of hunger—that to hold the world close was to crush it, perhaps, as a child crushes a moth while begging it not to leave. I opened my hands.

Nothing flew away.

Everything flew away.

The morning scattered into windows; the windows into rain; the rain into small, bright receipts no one had signed. I stood beneath them with my arms still curved around an absence warm from having been there, or almost there, or never there at all.

And the world turned in its sleep, blue and doorless, turned away, turned toward, turned away, while I whispered close, closer, no, not closer, only close, only—

close, close, close—

only, only—

close—

close—
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
